results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. The calyx is closest to the cortex and receives sensory interneuron afferents. The pedunculus is a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes. The mushroom body lobe system consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch, which have different structures at different life stages.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: There are multiple types of Kenyon cells in the adult Drosophila brain, including [KCab-c(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), [KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain"), [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, Kenyon cells can be classified into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which are further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and main classes. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain").

results.title: Gene expression
results.question: What neurotransmitter do mushroom body Kenyon cells use?
results.response: Mushroom body Kenyon cells, such as alpha/beta core Kenyon cells, use acetylcholine as their primary neurotransmitter. VFB records show that Kenyon cells are cholinergic, indicating they use acetylcholine.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response: The main components of the central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the paired noduli, the asymmetrical bodies, and the protocerebral bridge. These components are associated with functions including navigation/orientation, locomotor control, and sleep/arousal or memory-related behaviours.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111763 "Open lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") is located in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind, with distinct dendritic arbors in each lobula plate layer. It detects looming stimuli and projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. Its activity elicits a jump escape response. The dendritic arbors of LPLC2 span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells. There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe and they are cholinergic. In the lobula, LPLC2 has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4. VFB does not currently hold data on the full range of LPLC2's connections beyond its projection to the PVLP.

results.title: Comparative anatomy
results.question: How does the organisation of the antennal lobe compare between adult and larval Drosophila?
results.response: The organisation of the [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") in adult and larval Drosophila differs in terms of glomerular organization and tract connections. Both stages are glomerular, but the adult antennal lobe is represented as the more elaborated glomerular neuropil. VFB does not currently hold data on other aspects of the comparison between the adult and larval antennal lobe organisation.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response: The anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure is: DA1 glomerulus -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain. Alternatively, a more detailed hierarchy is: DA1 glomerulus -> adult olfactory antennal lobe glomerulus -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior. It has a large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum and a large descending axon, several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective. There is one giant fiber neuron per hemisphere. 

The giant fiber neuron is connected to various neurons, including the [adult VNC neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00059289 "Open adult VNC neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [thoracic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00001983 "Open thoracic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [secondary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047096 "Open secondary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch OFF hemilineage neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049540 "Open Notch OFF hemilineage neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [mesothoracic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00001985 "Open mesothoracic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [primary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047097 "Open primary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch OFF hemilineage secondary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049542 "Open Notch OFF hemilineage secondary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [prothoracic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00001984 "Open prothoracic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch ON hemilineage neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049539 "Open Notch ON hemilineage neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [NB2-4 lineage neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048927 "Open NB2-4 lineage neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch ON hemilineage secondary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049541 "Open Notch ON hemilineage secondary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [input/output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00053396 "Open input/output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain").

VFB has annotated 10 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the giant fiber neuron. 

Relevant publications include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and Power (1948).

results.title: Novel circuit exploration
results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response: The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") suggests that temperature information could influence memory formation. Thermosensory projection neurons relay temperature-detecting neurons to higher brain centers, and their connectivity includes mushroom-body-associated dopaminergic neurons and gamma main Kenyon cells. This indicates a plausible thermosensory influence on mushroom-body memory circuitry through thermosensory projection neurons. VFB holds records of various neuron types, including input/output neurons, projection neurons, and local neurons, but does not currently hold a comprehensive list of all connectivity partners between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body.

Connectomics data for the subesophageal zone can be explored through queries on neurons with parts in this region.

results.title: Concepts: NBLAST
results.question: What is NBLAST and what does an NBLAST similarity score mean?
results.response: NBLAST is a method used to calculate similarity scores, which represent the morphological similarity between neurons or expression patterns. An NBLAST similarity score is a measure of how similar a neuron is to another, based on its morphology. The score is calculated using NBLAST or other third-party scores.

results.title: API: REST endpoints
results.question: How can I query Virtual Fly Brain programmatically using the SOLR or Owlery API?
results.response: To query Virtual Fly Brain programmatically, you can use the Owlery API, which provides OWL reasoning services for Virtual Fly Brain's ontologies. The API endpoint is https://owl.virtualflybrain.org/ and it enables Description Logic queries, SPARQL queries with OWL reasoning, and access to multiple knowledgebases. Alternatively, you can use the SOLR Search API, which provides fast text search and autocomplete functionality for Virtual Fly Brain entities, datasets, and publications.

results.title: API: integrations
results.question: How do I explore Virtual Fly Brain neurons using Navis or pymaid?
results.response:
To explore Virtual Fly Brain neurons, you can use the pymaid library to connect to the VFB CATMAID server and retrieve neurons based on their ID or annotations. You can then use navis to plot the neurons. 
```
import pymaid
import navis

navis.set_pbars(jupyter=False)
pymaid.set_pbars(jupyter=False)

# Connect to the VFB CATMAID server hosting the FAFB data
rm = pymaid.connect_catmaid(server="https://fafb.catmaid.virtualflybrain.org/", api_token=None, max_threads=10)

# Find a neuron from its ID (16) -> this is an olfactory projection neuron
n = pymaid.get_neurons(16)

# Plot CatmaidNeuron with navis
navis.plot3d(n, width=1000, connectors=True, c='k')
```
VFB's documentation does not appear to cover Navis.

results.question: Where can I access the FAFB or FANC CATMAID datasets via Virtual Fly Brain?
results.response:
The FAFB CATMAID dataset can be accessed via https://fafb.catmaid.virtualflybrain.org. Virtual Fly Brain hosts several CATMAID instances for exploring connectomic reconstruction data, including the FAFB dataset. The FAFB CATMAID dataset information is available, with downloadable formats including obj, swc, nrrd, and wlz. 

The question about accessing the FANC CATMAID dataset remains unanswered, as the provided information does not mention it.

results.title: Anatomy teaching diagrams
results.question: Is there a circuit diagram of the mushroom body available on Virtual Fly Brain?
results.response: There is a schematic representation of the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") available on Virtual Fly Brain, which shows the compartmental organisation of the [adult mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003684 "Open adult mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") lobes, including how the dendrites of mushroom body output neurons and the axon terminals of dopaminergic neurons tile the lobes into a stereotyped grid of 15 compartments.
